newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr caps comeback with 2-month high.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr caps comeback with 2-month high.

text.p: The Australian dollar elbowed aside 78 cent resistance Monday to notch up its highest local close in almost two months.

The gains began late Friday when US$0.7738 support proved resilient to all pressure, encouraging enough offshore demand to squeeze 1/2 cent of gains out of a thin market. The momentum carried on today and dealers thought it only a matter of time before last week's intra-day peak around US$0.7820 was breached. Domestic trade data were regarded as favourable for the dollar with the goods and services deficit much narrower than expected, while inventory figures boded well for Q4 GDP.

"A sound trade performance means the AUD remains on track for 80 cents, especially with the 78 cent barrier breached in the last 24 hours," said Stephen Koukoulas, chief economist at Citibank Australia.
"Any significant upside to commodities on the back of the stronger world outlook could see that level reached and broken sooner rather than later," he added.

By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the currency was consolidating its beachhead at US$0.7815/20, the best local finish since January 8, after advancing from an early US$0.7795/00 and US$0.7750/55 late here Friday.

If US$0.7820 could be cleared, analysts favoured a rally to US$0.7880 which would mark a 50 percent retracement of the dollar's entire fall from a six-year peak of US$0.8212 in early December to last month's one-year low at US$0.7550.

The trend was even stronger on the crosses where the currency climbed to a fresh five year high on both the Swiss franc and German mark at 1.1565/88 and 1.3226/51 respectively from from 1.1422/37 and 1.3109/23 late Friday.
It also firmed to 94.28/38 yen from 93.21/31, although dealers were made cautious by talk Japanese investors were still looking to repatriate funds for their financial year-end.
All this added up to a 0.3 point rise in the trade weighted index to 59.6, not that distant from the December peak at 60.6.
Much of the recent recovery had come courtesy of an improving economic outlook which had greatly reduced the risk of another cut in official rates.
Today's data did nothing to challenge the upbeat outlook.

The balance on goods and services, a new release which replaces the notoriously volatile current account measure, showed a modest deficit of A$63 million in January compared to forecasts of a A$230 million shortfall. Both imports and exports were firm, boding well for an econmic pickup this year.

Data on private sector inventories showed a 1.2 percent rise in the December quarter, which was dead in line with forecasts. Downward revisions to past figures meant stocks would now only detract less than 0.1 point from GDP growth that quarter against forecasts of around 0.4 or 0.5 point.
This was timely for dollar bulls since a soft set of Q4 business investment data last week had suggested GDP growth could be lower than previously thought.
The GDP figures are released on Wednesday.
A more up-to-date reading on the economy will come from January retail sales and building approvals on Tuesday.

Sales, in particular, were disappointingly weak in December and analysts will be looking for some bounce back in January reflecting the surprise rate cut in December and anecdotal evidence from retailers.

If the strength is missing again the market could begin to wonder if another rate cut was really unthinkable. Forecasts favour a rise of 1.5 percent, but range from 0.2 to 3.0 percent, following December's 1.0 percent fall.
Building approvals are also expected to respond to signs of increased housing demand and rise 2.0 percent after a 1.0 percent fall in December. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
